description:
We are ÆR-OS, two developers from Argentina passionate about technology, innovation, and space exploration. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we're combining MODIS and VIIRS satellite data to track wildfire hotspots, identify historical patterns and anomalies, and improve fire monitoring and emergency response. Our mission is to transform complex satellite data into accessible tools that protect our planet.

From space data to Earth impact.
summary: Aeros turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into one comparable record. MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) do not see the same fires, so stacking the raw files makes activity jump by as much as 3.3 times when the satellite fleet changes, not when the fire does. We map every sensor onto a Suomi NPP–equivalent count on a common grid, using a monthly ratio plus a gradient-boosting correction that beats the ratio alone on held-out years and on regions it was not trained on. Location is never a model feature, so the method is not tied to one place. On that record, a web app lets anyone draw an area, see a month-by-year burning calendar from the early 2000s to today, compare a season with its own history, and download the result. It matters because Terra and Aqua are shutting down and Suomi NPP has already stopped: without a bridge across sensors, fire managers lose the baseline they need to tell a bad season from a change of satellite. We demonstrate it on the Gran Chaco (14.6 million detections).
details:
aeros turns twenty-six years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into one continuous record, then uses that record to show what is normal for a place and to warn people nearby when a new fire may be starting. It is live at https://aer-os.health (https://aer-os.health). The first study region is the Gran Chaco, across Argentina, Paraguay, and Bolivia. The harmonization never uses location as a model feature, so the method is not tied to that region.

What it does. FIRMS has tracked fire since 2000, but Terra and Aqua MODIS (1 km) and Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 VIIRS (375 m) do not see the same fires. Stacking the files makes the count jump when the satellite fleet changes. aeros puts every detection on a common H3 grid and translates MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent units, learned only where both sensors flew together. Suomi NPP defines the unit. NOAA-20 continues the record after Suomi NPP stopped delivering data, and NOAA-21 covers NOAA-20 outages. Each translation is checked by leaving out years and by holding out whole regions. The winning method is a simple ratio rule corrected by gradient boosting. On the Gran Chaco archive (about 14.6 million detections), that correction beats both the ratio alone and boosting alone, and a plain boosting model fails on land it has never seen. For any area and period the app shows a burning-activity calendar from the early 2000s to today, the anomaly against the same months in earlier years, a 90% interval, and a CSV download. A separate statistical test compares the last seven days of VIIRS detections with those same days in past years and flags a region when activity is at least twice the usual level. GOES-19 adds a fire layer that refreshes about every ten minutes. It never enters the harmonized record. When GOES-19 keeps a confident fire detection near a subscribed town, aeros sends a plain-language message by SMS, Telegram, or email, with distance, direction, and wind. The message says it is an early warning, not a confirmed fire.

Benefits and impact. Fire brigades, land managers, and local governments can tell whether a season was more active than the history of that place, instead of comparing incompatible sensors. People who live there get a timely notice between the infrequent passes of the polar satellites. The same method keeps the record usable as Terra and Aqua MODIS approach the end of their missions. A replay of the Corrientes fires shows the region rule would have flagged unusual activity on 18 December 2021, weeks before the worst of the 2022 season.

Tools. Python for the science pipeline (ingestion, H3 aggregation, validation, calendar, and scikit-learn models). TypeScript and React (Vite) for the web app, with deck.gl and three.js for the map and the Earth view. AWS CDK and Python Lambda functions for the API, the daily FIRMS refresh, and alerts. Data sources are NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m, archive and near real time), the GOES-19 ABI fire product, NASA POWER, Open-Meteo with ERA5, and public map imagery. Two people directed coding assistants. A person reviews every change. Nothing generative runs in the live product. Alerts are fixed text filled with measured numbers.

Why it is built this way. The team chose a result that can be measured where the sensors overlap, point data instead of heavy imagery, and a use that reaches both analysts and neighbors. Year and place are withheld from the model so it cannot memorize how much a cell usually burns. Uncertainty is shown next to every total. The calendar uses an accessible color ramp, and the interface speaks in everyday language. Raw satellite rows stay in the pipeline. People only see the processed record.
